来源：arXiv·核心检索（English）

原文发布：2026-11-02

本期推送：2026-11-03

TalkFlow: Structured Latent Flow Matching for Speech Driven Holistic Motion Generation

© cc

Abstract.

Holistic co-speech motion generation aims to synthesize coordinated facial expressions, hand gestures, and body movements from speech, which is challenging due to heterogeneous part-specific dynamics, long-range temporal coherence, and cross-part coordination. Directly modeling high-dimensional motion can be unstable, while overly compact or unstructured latent spaces may lose fine-grained motion details. We present TalkFlow, a structured latent flow framework for speech-driven holistic motion generation. TalkFlow learns a continuous three-stream latent representation for upper-body motion, lower-body motion, and facial expressions, preserving part-specific dynamics without forcing heterogeneous motion components into a single latent space. To maintain holistic coordination, lightweight cross-stream interactions are incorporated in both latent representation learning and flow-based generation. Conditioned on multi-level speech features, TalkFlow performs speech-conditioned latent flow matching, learning a continuous transport process from source latents to realistic motion latents. Experiments on the BEAT2 dataset demonstrate strong performance across facial expression accuracy, body gesture quality, and speech-motion synchronization. Qualitative comparisons and user studies further show that TalkFlow generates more natural, expressive, and speech-aligned holistic motion than state-of-the-art methods. The project page is available at https://xinmuwang.github.io/TalkFlow/.

Keywords:

Motion Generation, Flow Matching ††cc-license: by

1. Introduction

Generating expressive human motion from speech is a central problem for digital avatars, virtual agents, augmented and virtual reality, and embodied communication. With parametric human models such as SMPL-X [(Pavlakos et al., 2019)], holistic human motion can be represented in a unified form that includes body pose, hand articulation, and facial expressions. Recent co-speech datasets and benchmarks, such as BEAT2 [(Liu et al., 2024b)], further make it possible to study speech-driven 3D human motion at scale. However, generating realistic holistic motion remains challenging because speech-driven facial expressions, hand gestures, upper-body movements, and lower-body posture exhibit heterogeneous dynamics while requiring temporal coherence and cross-part coordination.

Existing co-speech motion generation methods have made significant progress. Early learning-based approaches mainly relied on deterministic regression [(Habibie et al., 2021; Ng et al., 2022)], which often averages over multiple plausible gestures. More recent methods improve diversity and realism through discrete latent modeling, masked modeling, diffusion, or sequence modeling architectures [(Yi et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2024b; Liu et al., 2024a; Chen et al., 2024; Xu et al., 2024a; Zhang et al., 2025b)]. Despite these advances, several limitations remain. Directly generating high-dimensional SMPL-X motion is difficult due to complex spatial–temporal dependencies. Latent generative models alleviate this issue, but overly compact or unstructured latent spaces may weaken fine-grained facial dynamics and body-part coordination. In particular, codebook-based motion latents introduce a discrete bottleneck that may cause quantization errors and limit the continuity required for subtle expression changes, smooth gesture transitions, and coordinated holistic motion. In addition, diffusion-based generation [(Ho et al., 2020)] often requires iterative denoising, which can be inefficient and may lead to inconsistent temporal evolution for long sequences.

To address these challenges, we propose TalkFlow, a structured latent flow framework for speech-driven holistic motion generation. TalkFlow first learns a compact continuous motion latent space using a structure-aware autoencoder, avoiding the discretization artifacts introduced by codebook-based motion tokens. The original SMPL-X axis-angle rotations are converted to the continuous 6D rotation representation [(Zhou et al., 2019)]. Rather than splitting the body before spatial encoding, TalkFlow first encodes the full SMPL-X pose graph with a holistic GCN to preserve global body topology. At the spatial encoding stage, full-body pose and facial expression are represented as two streams; the temporal encoder subsequently separates the pose representation into upper- and lower-body branches, yielding three bottleneck streams for upper-body motion, lower-body motion, and facial expressions.

The three-stream design preserves part-specific dynamics and avoids forcing heterogeneous motion components into a single latent space. Upper-body gestures are closely related to communicative intent and hand articulation, lower-body motion provides posture and global stability, and facial expressions capture fine-grained speech-related dynamics. However, these components are not independent in natural communication. We therefore introduce multi-stage cross-stream interactions in the autoencoder, including full pose–expression interaction before temporal compression, latent-level interaction among motion streams, and pose–expression interaction after temporal decoding. These interactions are implemented through lightweight FiLM-style [(Perez et al., 2018)] modulation and gated residual updates. This allows the model to exchange coordination cues across body and expression representations while preserving specialized stream dynamics.

Given speech input, TalkFlow performs generation through speech-conditioned latent flow matching [(Lipman et al., 2022)]. Multi-level acoustic and semantic features, including HuBERT [(Hsu et al., 2021)], Librosa [(McFee et al., 2015)], FastText [(Bojanowski et al., 2017)], and SBERT [(Reimers and Gurevych, 2019)], are encoded into branch-specific conditions for the three motion streams. The flow model learns a continuous transport process from source latents to realistic motion latents using stream-specific Transformer branches, speech condition attention, and lightweight FiLM-gated cross-stream coordination. This design enables efficient latent-space generation while maintaining temporal coherence and holistic motion consistency.

By combining holistic graph-based motion encoding, continuous three-stream latent representation learning, and speech-conditioned latent flow matching, TalkFlow generates expressive and coordinated talking human motion. Experiments on the BEAT2 dataset [(Liu et al., 2024b)] demonstrate strong facial fidelity, competitive body-gesture quality, and effective speech-motion synchronization under the standard Speaker-2 evaluation protocol. Qualitative comparisons and user studies further show that TalkFlow produces more natural, speech-aligned, and perceptually preferred holistic motion compared with existing methods.

We summarize our main contributions as follows:

  • •

    We propose TalkFlow, a structured latent flow framework for speech-driven holistic motion generation that synthesizes coordinated facial expressions, upper-body gestures, and lower-body motion from speech.

  • •

    We introduce a continuous structure-aware three-stream motion representation that encodes the full-body SMPL-X pose graph and models upper-body motion, lower-body motion, and facial expressions with separate but interactive temporal streams.

  • •

    We formulate speech-driven holistic motion generation as speech-conditioned latent flow matching, using branch-specific speech conditions and a three-stream velocity backbone to achieve strong facial fidelity, competitive holistic motion performance, and improved perceptual quality on BEAT2 [(Liu et al., 2024b)].

    • 2. Related Work

    2.1. Co-speech and holistic motion generation.

    Human motion generation can be conditioned on text, audio, scene context, or other control signals [(Zhu et al., 2023)]. Among them, speech-driven motion generation is most relevant to our work, as it requires motion to follow both acoustic dynamics and communicative semantics. Early co-speech systems relied on rule-based gesture mappings [(Cassell et al., 2001; Kopp and Wachsmuth, 2004; Levine et al., 2010; Poggi et al., 2005)], while learning-based methods later modeled either facial animation [(Cudeiro et al., 2019; Fan et al., 2022; Peng et al., 2023; Shen et al., 2023)] or body gestures [(Ginosar et al., 2019; Yoon et al., 2020; Liu et al., 2022d; Yang et al., 2023; Ao et al., 2023)]. These part-specific approaches often struggle to maintain coordination across face, hands, and body. Recent holistic methods address this issue by jointly modeling multiple motion components. Habibie et al. [(Habibie et al., 2021)] used a shared audio encoder with separate body-part decoders, TalkSHOW [(Yi et al., 2023)] combined probabilistic gesture generation with facial animation, DiffSHEG [(Chen et al., 2024)] introduced directed face-to-body information flow, and EMAGE [(Liu et al., 2024b)] used masked gesture reconstruction and audio-conditioned synthesis. MambaTalk [(Xu et al., 2024a)] and EchoMask [(Zhang et al., 2025b)] further explored efficient temporal modeling and speech-guided masked motion generation, while SemTalk [(Zhang et al., 2025a)] emphasizes frame-level semantic cues for holistic co-speech motion generation. More recently, EchoAvatar [(Chen et al., 2026)] targets real-time full-body avatar animation from streaming audio. Despite these advances, preserving part-specific dynamics and holistic coordination remains challenging.

    2.2. Latent representations for holistic motion.

    Latent motion representations are widely used to reduce the complexity of high-dimensional motion generation. VQ-VAE [(Van Den Oord et al., 2017)] and PQ-VAE [(Wu and Flierl, 2019; Jegou et al., 2010)] provide compact discrete motion priors and have been adopted in co-speech generation. ProbTalk [(Liu et al., 2024a)] represents facial and upper-body motion in a shared discrete latent space, while Combo [(Xu et al., 2024b)] introduces part-aware latent decomposition and interaction. HoloDiff [(Wang et al., 2026)] performs speech-conditioned diffusion in a structured latent space for holistic talking human animation. Building on structured latent modeling, TalkFlow learns continuous upper-body, lower-body, and expression streams and coordinates them through lightweight FiLM-gated interactions, preserving part-specific dynamics without relying on discrete motion tokens.

    2.3. Flow-based generative motion modeling.

    Flow-based generative models have also been explored for motion synthesis. MoGlow [(Henter et al., 2020)] introduced normalizing flows for probabilistic and controllable motion generation. More recently, Flow Matching [(Lipman et al., 2022)] and Rectified Flow [(Liu et al., 2022a)] provide efficient continuous-time formulations for learning generative transport dynamics. In motion generation, Motion Flow Matching [(Hu et al., 2023)] applies flow matching to text- and action-conditioned human motion, and MotionLab [(Guo et al., 2025)] further studies flow-based human motion generation and editing in a unified framework. FLOAT [(Ki et al., 2025)] demonstrates motion latent flow matching for audio-driven talking portraits, while FlowerDance [(Yang et al., 2025)] explores efficient flow-based generation for music-driven dance synthesis. These works show the potential of flow-based generation, but they mainly focus on locomotion, text/action-conditioned motion, editing, dance, or talking portrait animation. TalkFlow instead applies latent flow matching to holistic 3D co-speech motion using branch-specific speech conditions and interacting upper-body, lower-body, and expression streams.

    3. Method

    3.1. Problem Definition

    Given a speech clip of length N, our goal is to generate a sequence of holistic talking human motions that are temporally aligned with the speech signal. We adopt SMPL-X [(Pavlakos et al., 2019)] as the motion representation, which models facial expressions, hand gestures, and full-body poses in a unified parametric form.

    Let A=[a₁,…,a_N] denote the input speech features. The target motion consists of articulated body poses and facial expressions. The pose sequence is denoted as R=[r₁,…,r_N], where each pose is represented using the continuous Rot6D representation [(Zhou et al., 2019)]. Facial expressions are represented by blendshape coefficients E=[e₁,…,e_N]. Each frame contains 55×6 pose rotations and 100 expression coefficients. To model heterogeneous body dynamics, we decompose the body pose into upper-body and lower-body components:

    (1)

    R={Rᵘ,Rˡ},

    where Rᵘ includes upper-body and hand joints, and Rˡ includes lower-body joints. Our objective is to learn a speech-conditioned generative model:

    (2)

    p(Rᵘ,Rˡ,E|A),

    which produces coordinated upper-body motion, lower-body motion, and facial expressions.

    3.2. Data Preprocessing

    We preprocess the BEAT2 motion, audio, and text data into temporally aligned training clips. For motion data, we use SMPL-X pose and expression parameters, where the original axis-angle pose rotations are converted into the continuous 6D rotation representation [(Zhou et al., 2019)]. We segment each sequence into 240-frame clips with a 60-frame overlap. Since BEAT2 is captured at 30 FPS, each clip corresponds to 8 seconds of motion and is encoded into a latent sequence of length 60 with a temporal downsampling factor of 4. The 60-frame overlap is used for training-clip construction and is distinct from the 8-frame overlap used for long-sequence inference. For audio conditioning, we extract HuBERT features [(Hsu et al., 2021)] and handcrafted Librosa features [(McFee et al., 2015)] offline and align them with the motion clips. For textual conditioning, following MambaTalk [(Xu et al., 2024a)], we pre-extract word-level FastText embeddings [(Bojanowski et al., 2017)] and sentence-level SBERT embeddings [(Reimers and Gurevych, 2019)] from aligned transcripts, which are used as auxiliary conditioning signals together with audio features.

    TalkFlow follows a two-stage design, as shown in Figure 2. The first stage learns a continuous structured motion space that reduces the complexity of high-dimensional SMPL-X motion while preserving part-specific dynamics and holistic coordination. The second stage performs speech-conditioned generation in this learned latent space using flow matching, allowing the flow model to operate on compact, interaction-aware motion latents.

    3.3. Stage I: Structured Three-Stream Motion Autoencoder

    We learn a structured continuous latent space for upper-body motion, lower-body motion, and facial expressions. A key design choice is to preserve full-body spatial topology before temporal decomposition. Instead of encoding upper- and lower-body poses independently from the beginning, we first encode the complete SMPL-X pose graph with a holistic graph encoder, so that global body structure and cross-limb dependencies are retained before the motion is separated into temporal streams. The graph topology follows the anatomical design of Pose2Mesh [(Choi et al., 2020)]; detailed topology construction is provided in the supplementary material. We use Chebyshev graph convolutions [(Defferrard et al., 2016)] in the pose encoder, while facial expressions are encoded by a lightweight frame-level MLP. Thus, the spatial encoding stage is initially pose–expression two-stream, whereas the compressed bottleneck is upper–lower–expression three-stream.

    Given a motion sequence (R,E), the spatial encoders produce

    (3)

    (Hᵖ,Hᵖ_g)=G_ψ(R), Hᵉ=M_ψ(E),

    where the graph encoder produces frame-level node features hᵖₜ∈ℝ^55×64 and global pose features hᵖ_g,t∈ℝ¹²⁸. Their temporal stacks are denoted by Hᵖ=[hᵖ₁,…,hᵖ_T] and Hᵖ_g=[hᵖ_g,1,…,hᵖ_g,T], respectively.

    After spatial pose–expression interaction, the updated features H̃ᵖ and H̃ᵉ are routed to three temporal branches:

    (4)

    Zᵘ=Tᵘ_ψ(H̃ᵖ), Zˡ=Tˡ_ψ(H̃ᵖ), Zᵉ=Tᵉ_ψ(H̃ᵉ).

    Here, Zᵘ, Zˡ, and Zᵉ are continuous latents for upper-body motion, lower-body motion, and facial expressions, respectively. The temporal encoder downsamples the sequence by a factor of f, resulting in T^′=T/f latent tokens. This decomposition avoids forcing heterogeneous motion components into one latent space: upper-body gestures, lower-body posture, and facial expressions exhibit different temporal dynamics and relationships to speech. The shared spatial encoder and interaction modules retain holistic structure, while the temporal branches preserve part-specific dynamics.

    The decoder reconstructs upper- and lower-body pose features, merges them into a full-body representation, and outputs the original SMPL-X pose and expression:

    (5)

    R̂,Ê=D_ψ(Zᵘ,Zˡ,Zᵉ).

    Although the three-stream representation preserves part-specific dynamics, independently encoding these streams would weaken holistic coordination. All interaction modules use FiLM-style modulation [(Perez et al., 2018)] and gated residual updates. Given a target feature x and a temporally aligned conditioning feature c, we define

    (6)h=φ(c),
    (γ,β,g)=(W_γh, W_βh, σ(W_gh)),
    F(x,c)=x+α g⊙(γ⊙x+β),
    ℝ(x,c)=x+α g⊙W_Δh.

    where F and ℝ denote the FiLM-gated and residual-gated updates, φ(·) is a lightweight projection, and α is a learnable scalar initialized to a small value. For node-wise pose features, the modulation parameters are broadcast across the joint dimension.

    At the spatial stage, expression features modulate pose-node features through F; the updated pose nodes are pooled and softly blended with the global pose feature, which then updates the expression stream through ℝ. At the bottleneck, interactions are applied bidirectionally between upper–lower and upper–expression streams, while direct lower–expression interaction is omitted. After temporal decoding, a final pose–expression interaction is applied before the output decoders. This design coordinates the streams without collapsing them into a single latent representation.

    The autoencoder is optimized with reconstruction and temporal consistency losses:

    (7)

    L_AE=L_rec+λᵥₑₗLᵥₑₗ+λ_accL_acc,

    where L_rec supervises pose and expression reconstruction, and Lᵥₑₗ and L_acc enforce first- and second-order temporal consistency. After training, the autoencoder is frozen and used to provide structured target latents and the decoder for speech-conditioned flow generation.

    3.4. Stage II: Speech-Conditioned Latent Flow Matching

    Stage II generates motion by learning a speech-conditioned transport process in the structured latent space. Compared with direct motion-space generation, latent flow matching reduces the dimensionality and improves stability. Compared with codebook-based generation, it preserves a continuous motion representation and avoids quantization artifacts. The learned velocity field is integrated by an ODE solver to transport source latents to realistic motion latents.

    Given the pre-extracted HuBERT, Librosa, FastText, and SBERT features, we construct branch-specific speech conditions:

    (8)

    Cᵘ,Cˡ,Cᵉ=ℂ_ω(Aʰ,Aʳ,Tʷ,Tᵍ),

    where Aʰ and Aʳ denote HuBERT and Librosa audio features, and Tʷ and Tᵍ denote word-level FastText and sentence-level SBERT features. The condition encoder produces separate conditions because facial expressions depend more strongly on phonetic and semantic content, upper-body gestures respond to prosody and communicative emphasis, and lower-body motion mainly reflects posture and stability. It uses branch-specific audio/text projections, semantic modulation, residual gating, and temporal downsampling to produce conditions aligned with the latent resolution.

    Let

    (9)

    Z₁={Zᵘ₁,Zˡ₁,Zᵉ₁}

    denote target latents obtained from the frozen autoencoder. We independently sample source latents:

    (10)

    Z₀={Zᵘ₀,Zˡ₀,Zᵉ₀}, Zˢ₀∼ℕ(0,I), s∈{u,l,e}.

    Although ODE integration is deterministic for a fixed Z₀, different Gaussian source latents produce different transport trajectories and generated motions. For τ∼U(0,1), we construct the interpolated latent and target velocity:

    (11)

    Z_τ=(1-τ)Z₀+τZ₁, U_τ=Z₁-Z₀.

    The flow model uses a three-stream Transformer backbone to predict velocities for the structured latent streams. Each stream performs speech-condition cross-attention with its corresponding branch-specific condition, while the motion streams exchange information through the FiLM-gated interaction defined above. We use the interaction neighborhoods ℕ(u)={l,e}, ℕ(l)={u}, and ℕ(e)={u}. The velocity prediction for stream s is

    (12)

    Û_τˢ=V_θˢ (Z_τˢ,τ,Cˢ;{Z_τʳ}_r∈ℕ(s)), s∈{u,l,e}.

    Thus, ℂ={Cᵘ,Cˡ,Cᵉ} contains three branch-specific conditions rather than one shared condition.

    The latent flow matching objective is

    (13)

    L_FM=∑_s∈{u,l,e}λₛ𝔼_τ,Z₀,Z₁[∥Û_τˢ-U_τˢ∥₂²].

    To improve compatibility between the learned latent flow and the frozen decoder, we integrate the learned field from Z₀ to obtain Z̃₁, decode it through the frozen Stage-I decoder, and supervise the resulting pose and expression in the original motion space:

    (14)

    L_gen=L_FM+λᵣₒₗₗLᵣₒₗₗ.

    This rollout loss constrains the integrated trajectory after decoding and improves motion-space fidelity and temporal stability.

    During inference, the condition encoder first produces {Cᵘ,Cˡ,Cᵉ} from the input speech. Source latents are then integrated from τ=0 to τ=1 and decoded into SMPL-X motion. We use fixed-step Euler integration with 50 function evaluations. For arbitrary-length generation, 240-frame windows overlap by 8 original motion frames. The final overlap of the previous window is used as known context for the next window; overlapping predictions are linearly blended and smoothed with a Gaussian kernel of size 3 to reduce boundary discontinuities. This stitching is confined to the overlap region and is used only for long-sequence inference.

    3.5. Training details.

    The structured autoencoder is trained first and then frozen. The flow backbone is first optimized with L_FM and subsequently fine-tuned with L_gen. We use temporal compression 4×, latent dimensions (d_zᵘ,d_zˡ,d_zᵉ)=(512,128,512), condition dimensions (d_cᵘ,d_cˡ,d_cᵉ)=(256,128,384), a 6-layer/8-head Transformer backbone with hidden dimension 384, and interaction hidden dimension 256. With pre-extracted speech features, Euler sampling with 50 NFEs runs at 0.006 s per frame on one RTX 4070 Ti SUPER. Remaining optimization and implementation details are provided in the supplementary material.

    4. Experiments

    4.1. Experimental Settings

    4.1.1. Dataset.

    For training and evaluation, we use the BEAT2 dataset [(Liu et al., 2024b)], which contains 60 hours of high-quality motion data from 25 speakers, including 12 female and 13 male speakers. The dataset consists of 1,762 sequences, with an average duration of 65.66 seconds, where speakers respond to daily inquiries. We divide the dataset into training, validation, and test sets with ratios of 85%, 7.5%, and 7.5%, respectively. To ensure a fair comparison with prior work, we follow EMAGE [(Liu et al., 2024b)] and use the Speaker-2 subset for training, validation, and testing. This single-speaker protocol provides a controlled evaluation setting, but it also limits the range of speaker-specific gesture styles observed during training.

    4.1.2. Metrics.

    We evaluate generated body gestures using Fréchet Gesture Distance (FGD) [(Yoon et al., 2020)], which measures the distributional distance between generated and ground-truth gestures. We compute FGD using the feature extractor provided by the official EMAGE codebase. Following EMAGE [(Liu et al., 2024b)], DIV [(Li et al., 2021a)] is computed as the average L1 distance between generated gesture clips, and therefore mainly reflects coordinate-level motion variation. To evaluate speech-motion synchrony, we use Beat Consistency Score (BCS) [(Li et al., 2021b)], which measures the temporal alignment between gesture rhythm and low-level audio beats. For facial motion evaluation, we report vertex mean squared error (MSE) and vertex L1 difference (LVD) [(Yi et al., 2023)], which measure the discrepancy between generated and ground-truth facial vertices. Since quantitative metrics may not fully capture semantic appropriateness and perceptual naturalness, we further conduct qualitative comparisons and a user perception study.

    4.2. Quantitative Results

    As shown in Table 1, TalkFlow achieves the best facial MSE and LVD, together with the second-best FGD and BCS. The improvements in MSE and LVD indicate that the structured latent representation preserves fine-grained facial dynamics. ProbTalk obtains a slightly higher BCS, whereas TalkFlow performs better on FGD, DIV, MSE, and LVD. These results also indicate that no single metric provides a complete measure of holistic generation quality. Combo [(Xu et al., 2024b)] is not included because its results use a different four-subject train/test protocol, and its code and pretrained models are unavailable for retraining under the common Speaker-2 setting.

    For body gesture evaluation, TalkFlow achieves the second-best FGD. FGD evaluates distributional similarity in a learned gesture feature space, but does not directly measure perceptual realism, semantic appropriateness, or face–body coordination. EchoMask obtains the lowest FGD, whereas TalkFlow obtains the lowest mean realism rank in the user study. This difference suggests that feature-distribution distance and perceived motion quality capture complementary aspects of generation performance.

    BCS measures low-level coincidence between audio and motion beats. Notably, the ground-truth BCS of 6.86 is lower than that of every holistic generation method in Table 1. Therefore, a higher BCS does not necessarily imply more natural or semantically appropriate motion and may favor frequent or regular beat responses. In contrast, the user study evaluates perceived speech-motion synchronization at a higher perceptual level, where TalkFlow obtains the lowest mean rank among the evaluated methods. BCS should thus be interpreted as a low-level rhythmic alignment metric rather than a standalone measure of overall synchronization quality.

    TalkFlow obtains a lower quantitative DIV than several baselines. Since DIV is computed from L1 distances between generated gesture clips, it mainly reflects coordinate-level motion variation rather than high-level diversity of gesture patterns, expressive modes, or talking styles. This distinction is reflected in the user study: MambaTalk obtains the lowest mean diversity rank, while TalkFlow ranks second, despite their lower quantitative DIV than TalkSHOW and EchoMask. Flow matching is not inherently deterministic, because different Gaussian source latents produce different generation trajectories. However, the current model uses a simple white-noise prior without explicit talking-style conditioning, and the Speaker-2 protocol contains limited style variation. Style-conditioned priors and multi-speaker training may therefore further improve controllable diversity.

    4.3. Ablation Study

    Table 2 validates the contribution of the main components in TalkFlow. The single-latent variant compresses all motion components into one shared latent space. Separating pose and expression in the dual-latent variant improves facial MSE/LVD from 7.20/7.76 to 6.66/7.16, while also improving FGD, BCS, and DIV. The triple-latent variants further decompose full-body pose into upper- and lower-body streams, producing a substantial reduction in FGD and confirming the benefit of preserving heterogeneous part-specific dynamics.

    Introducing autoencoder-stage interaction further improves both body and facial metrics, indicating that coordination during representation learning benefits holistic motion generation. The full model achieves the best results across all ablation metrics, showing that graph-based pose encoding, autoencoder and flow-stage interactions, and ODE rollout reconstruction are complementary. In particular, removing rollout reconstruction substantially degrades FGD, confirming that motion-space rollout supervision improves compatibility between the learned latent trajectory and the frozen decoder.

    4.4. User Perception Study

    Following the user study protocol of EchoMask [(Zhang et al., 2025b)], we conduct a perceptual evaluation to compare the visual quality and speech-motion consistency of different methods. We recruit 37 participants with normal or corrected-to-normal vision, normal hearing, and sufficient English proficiency to understand the evaluated speech clips. Participants are asked to rank generated videos from different methods according to four perceptual criteria: realism, semantic consistency, speech-motion synchronization, and motion diversity. We report the average rank for each method, where a lower rank indicates stronger user preference.

    As shown in Fig. 3, TalkFlow obtains the lowest mean rank in realism, semantic consistency, and speech-motion synchronization. These perceptual results complement rather than replace the quantitative metrics. Although EchoMask obtains a lower FGD in Table 1, TalkFlow receives a lower mean realism rank, illustrating that FGD does not fully capture motion naturalness, temporal stability, and holistic coordination.

    For speech-motion synchronization, TalkFlow obtains the lowest mean user-study rank among the evaluated methods, while its quantitative BCS is second-best. This difference is consistent with the distinct aspects captured by the two evaluations: BCS measures low-level audio-beat coincidence, whereas participants evaluate whether generated gestures and facial motion appear appropriately synchronized with the speech as a whole. The comparatively low ground-truth BCS further shows that maximizing beat coincidence is not equivalent to maximizing perceived synchronization.

    For motion diversity, MambaTalk obtains the lowest mean rank and TalkFlow ranks second. This differs from quantitative DIV, where both methods score below TalkSHOW and EchoMask. DIV reflects coordinate-level variation and therefore does not necessarily capture high-level variation in gesture patterns, expressive modes, or talking styles. The user-study results suggest that TalkFlow retains perceptually meaningful motion variation despite its lower coordinate-level DIV.

    Participant comments further support these observations. EMAGE often produces body movements that are too calm and do not fully match the agitated tone of the speech; however, its conservative motion also avoids severe torso deformation. MambaTalk exhibits the largest range of body movement and often matches the angry tone well, but participants also observe occasional unnatural jitters and sudden full-body twists. EchoMask sometimes produces repetitive arm postures, and its wrists may appear unnatural. In contrast, TalkFlow is generally perceived as the most balanced method, with smoother pose transitions, more stable body motion, and better synchronization with the speech tempo.

    4.5. Qualitative Results

    We provide qualitative comparisons with representative holistic co-speech motion generation methods in the final two figure-only pages to allow larger rendered frames and clearer visual inspection. We first compare facial motion at selected spoken words in Fig. 4. Since BEAT2 facial motion is generally close to neutral and SMPL-X provides a relatively sparse facial representation, differences in static renderings are mainly visible through lip opening/closing and mouth-motion timing. TalkFlow generally produces mouth shapes closest to the ground truth, while several baseline results contain clear lip-shape errors, such as an open mouth when the ground-truth mouth is closed. Red boxes mark only these evident errors; unboxed results are not assigned a binary correct/incorrect label.

    We further compare body motion on 14 word-level cases in Fig. 5 and  6. Each case corresponds to the body pose generated at a specific spoken word, allowing direct comparison of gesture timing, body posture, and face–body coordination under the same speech context. Orange boxes highlight representative ground-truth motion regions used as visual references, green boxes indicate generated motions closest to the corresponding references, and red boxes mark visible artifacts or semantically inconsistent motions. In most selected cases, TalkFlow remains close to the ground truth while avoiding obvious artifacts such as implausible body deformation, abrupt large movements, or unstable poses.

    5. Conclusion

    We presented TalkFlow, a structured latent flow framework for speech-driven holistic motion generation. TalkFlow learns a continuous three-stream latent representation for upper-body motion, lower-body motion, and facial expressions, avoiding both direct high-dimensional motion generation and discrete tokenization. By encoding the full-body pose graph before temporal stream separation and coordinating the streams through lightweight FiLM-gated interactions, TalkFlow preserves part-specific dynamics while maintaining holistic face–body consistency.

    We further introduced speech-conditioned latent flow matching to generate coordinated motion latents from acoustic and textual speech features. Experiments on BEAT2 show that TalkFlow achieves the best facial fidelity and competitive body-motion performance. Qualitative comparisons demonstrate plausible word-level lip dynamics and natural body gestures with fewer visible artifacts. The user study further shows that TalkFlow obtains the lowest mean rank in realism, semantic consistency, and speech-motion synchronization, together with the largest overall share of first-place rankings.

    Several limitations remain. The single-speaker Speaker-2 protocol limits evidence for cross-speaker and cross-style generalization. The current Gaussian prior also lacks explicit talking-style control, limiting controllable diversity. Moreover, global translation is not modeled, making foot–ground contact difficult to constrain and contributing to occasional foot sliding. Future work will explore multi-speaker training, style-conditioned latent priors, and joint global-translation/contact constraints for more diverse and physically plausible motion.

    （参考文献见原文。）

item.title: 形状抽象要既像又能读：SemEllipsoid 用椭球集合做语义一致的分层抽象，一个部件只属于一个语义 ｜ SemEllipsoid: Semantic-aware Shape Abstraction with Ellipsoid
item.description:
一句话：每个椭球严格对应单一语义部件，不跨语义分配；同一输入可给多档抽象层级。

要点：

  • 目标：用一组椭球基元表示 3D 形状，既要在几何上忠实，又要在语义上可读（这类表示常被称作「知识驱动的抽象」）
  • 关键约束很硬：每个基元**严格只对应一个语义部件**，不允许跨语义分配——这正是多数基元拟合方法做不到的
  • 同一输入可给出不同粒度的抽象层级，便于在不同细节需求下复用

为什么值得看：代理体（proxy）、碰撞体、LOD 低模、物理简化都有同一个需求：用少量基元概括形状且部件别串味。把语义约束加进拟合，等于让抽象结果天然对齐引擎里的部件划分。

中文摘要：用一组基元（椭球、盒子等）来表示 3D 形状是图形学里的经典做法，但多数拟合方法只追求几何误差，产出的基元经常跨部件混在一起，读起来没有语义。SemEllipsoid 提出语义感知的形状抽象：给定任意类别的 3D 形状，输出一组既几何忠实、又语义一致的椭球；关键约束是每个基元严格只对应单一语义部件，不允许跨语义分配，同时同一输入可以给出不同粒度的抽象层级。对代理体、碰撞体与 LOD 简化这类需要「少量基元概括形状」的场景，语义一致意味着结果能直接对齐引擎里的部件划分。

主题：图形学

来源：arXiv·核心检索（English）

原文发布：2026-11-02

本期推送：2026-11-03

SemEllipsoid: Semantic-aware Shape Abstraction with Ellipsoid

Abstract.

Representing 3D shapes using a set of primitives–known as shape abstraction–is an actively studied problem in computer graphics. with wide applications in shape understanding, analysis, and simulation due to the compactness and computational efficiency of the primitive-based representation. Prior work has primarily focused on geometry-aware shape abstraction, where the objective is to approximate the input shape with a minimal set of primitives while preserving geometric fidelity. However, these methods often overlook semantic consistency, inevitably leading to primitives that span across multiple semantic parts. Such inconsistency can cause undesirable artifacts in downstream tasks such as part-level shape editing or manipulation. In this paper, we introduce a new task - semantic-aware shape abstraction, where the goal is to produce abstractions that are both geometrically faithful and semantically consistent, ensuring that each primitive adheres strictly to a single semantic part without crossing semantic boundaries. We propose SemEllipsoid, a novel method to address this problem using ellipsoidal primitives. The core idea is to inject semantic constraints into the primitive optimization process leveraging the availability of semantic cues from large-scale foundation models. We design a fully differentiable projection–blending–evaluation scheme to measure semantic divergence against input semantic masks, and formulate an alternating optimization strategy to iteratively solve for optimal semantic assignment and primitive configurations. Our method is non-learning-based, requiring no data collection or network training, and generalizes well to shapes from arbitrary categories. It also supports different levels of abstraction according to user demand. Extensive experiments and evaluations validate the effectiveness of our approach across several 3D shape collections.

Keywords:

Shape Abstraction, Semantic Injection, Primitives, Ellipsoid, Differentiable Projection-Blending-Evaluation

1. Introduction

Humans perceive real-world objects by effortlessly recognizing their structure by parts and part semantics, serving as important cues for many purposes, like human-object interaction and object functionality analysis. The structure can be represented as a composition of simple primitives (e.g., spheres, ellipsoids, boxes) with clear semantics. The decomposition and abstraction process, also known as Shape Abstraction, has been an active research field for decades in computer graphics. The abstract shape, its structures, and part semantics play an essential role in downstream tasks, such as shape geometry, structure and functionality analysis [(Mitra et al., 2014; Hu et al., 2018)], shape editing [(Yumer et al., 2015)], shape retrieval and manipulation [(Sun et al., 2019)], object grasping [(Vezzani et al., 2017; Vezzani et al., 2018)], and motion planning [(Ruan et al., 2022)].

Existing research solves this problem from different aspects - computational optimization [(Chevalier et al., 2003; Vaskevicius and Birk, 2017)], deep learning [(Tulsiani et al., 2017; Sun et al., 2019; Zhao et al., 2024)], to name a few. More recent work (e.g., PrimitiveAnything [(Ye et al., 2025)], PartGen [(Chen et al., 2025a)]) reformulates this task as shape-conditioned primitive generation. Their training is performed on a human-annotated large-scale dataset, improving the generalization ability greatly. The primary focus of prior work is geometry-aware shape abstraction, where the objective is to approximate the input shape with a minimal set of primitives while preserving geometric fidelity. However, these methods often overlook semantic consistency, inevitably leading to primitives that span across multiple semantic parts. Such inconsistency can cause undesirable artifacts in downstream tasks such as part-level shape editing or manipulation. Figure 2 presents such an example, where Marching-Primitives [(Liu et al., 2023a)] outputs a superquadrics abstraction of the back leg, spanning from the leg to the back (Fig. 2(a)). A follow-up part-based shape editing produces undesired artifacts (Fig. 2(b)).

In this paper, we propose a new task–semantic-aware shape abstraction, where the goal is to produce abstractions that are both geometrically faithful and semantically consistent, ensuring that each primitive adheres strictly to a single semantic part without crossing semantic boundaries (see Fig. 2(c)). Two core challenges exist to achieve this goal: i) where to obtain the semantic information, and ii) how to inject the semantic cues during shape abstraction. We draw inspiration from the rapid advancement of large foundation models. For example, Segment Anything Model (SAM) [(Kirillov et al., 2023)] and DINO [(Zhang et al., 2022)] can produce part semantics robustly and accurately, making semantic information readily accessible in a category-agnostic and open-vocabulary manner.

Based on this insight, we present a novel approach, dubbed SemEllipsoid, for semantic-aware shape abstraction with ellipsoids. Our approach falls into the category of geometrical optimization-based shape abstraction, and we achieve semantic injection by formulating it as a semantic penalty loss term in the optimization. Specifically, given an input 3D shape together with multi-view semantic masks, we first initialize a set of ellipsoid primitives to approximate the input. In the following optimization, we aim to simultaneously find the optimal primitive parameters and semantic labels, such that the primitives resemble the shape with high geometric fidelity while strictly adhering to semantic constraints.

To measure the semantic discrepancy, we choose to project the ellipsoid to the semantic masks. However, primitives inside the shape volume occlude and overlap with each other. Naive projection will simply disable the optimization for inside primitives. Inspired by the alpha blending operator in differentiable rendering and shape optimization [(Liu et al., 2019; Laine et al., 2020; Yuan et al., 2024)], we propose an innovative differentiable projection-blending-evaluation scheme to penalize the semantic violation. Given the non-linear and non-convex nature of the optimization due to the integer variables of labels and continuous variables of primitives, we solve it iteratively in an alternating way, i.e., label assignment and primitive optimization. After the optimization, an optional post-merging step can further group primitives possessing the same semantic label, producing multi-level abstractions according to user intentions.

Our method significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods, and extensive experiments, ablation studies, and discussions validate our design choices, effectiveness, and scalability. To summarize, the principal contributions of this work include:

  • •

    We propose semantic-aware shape abstraction, a new task for both geometrically faithful and semantically consistent shape abstraction.

  • •

    We propose the first approach-SemEllipsoid, which is simple, neat, and effective for solving this new problem. Our approach can handle various shape categories without any label-intensive data processing and network training, and it can produce multi-level shape abstractions, facilitating various downstream tasks.

  • •

    Our projection-blending-evaluation technical design effectively injects semantic cues in a differentiable way, and might inspire future research.

    • 2. Related Works

    Shape abstraction.

    The goal of traditional shape abstraction is to represent a 3D shape using the smallest possible set of simple primitives while preserving the closest possible approximation of the original geometry. Computational approaches typically frame this as a problem of fitting primitives to the input geometry [(Gross and Boult, 1988; Solina and Bajcsy, 1990; Leonardis et al., 1997; Chevalier et al., 2003; Vaskevicius and Birk, 2017; Park et al., 2025)] or estimating primitive parameters using Bayesian methods [(Liu et al., 2022; Wu et al., 2022a; Liu et al., 2023a)]. Superquadrics are widely used as primitives in computational methods. It encodes common primitives like spheres, cuboids, and cylinders with only five parameters, resulting in strong expressiveness and desirable analytical properties. Another group of work focuses on learning-based approaches. Methods from [(Tulsiani et al., 2017; Sun et al., 2019; Zhao et al., 2024; Yang and Chen, 2021; Hao et al., 2020; Yu et al., 2024; Fedele et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2020; Deng et al., 2020)] address the task in an unsupervised setting, aiming to learn an optimal abstraction strategy for shapes within a specific category. The core objective of both the computational and learning-based methods is to approximate the shape in high fidelity, not necessarily producing abstractions with human-intuitive semantics.

    Part-based 3D shape generation.

    Part-based 3D shape generation is an emerging topic, with concurrent works like PartGen [(Chen et al., 2025a)], AutoPartGen [(Chen et al., 2025b)], PrimitiveAnything [(Ye et al., 2025)], PartCrafter [(Ng et al., 2024)], PartPacker [(Tang et al., 2025)], LLM-Primitives [(Tian et al., 2025)], and OmniPart [(Yang et al., 2025)]. These methods can directly generate semantically meaningful parts conditioned on image or text inputs. However, on the one hand, since they do not enforce semantic-awareness, their parts might overlap, leading to semantic violation. On the other hand, their generalization depends on certain datasets. In contrast, we explicitly enforce semantic awareness in our optimization, which can be applied to any input shape without any training process. Please refer to the comparison section for a detailed analysis.

    3D Shape part segmentation

    A branch of methods has been developed to decompose a 3D shape into semantically meaningful and geometrically coherent parts. Co-segmentation methods take as input a family of shapes within a category and produce their part segmentations simultaneously [(Paschalidou et al., 2021; Chen et al., 2024; Hu et al., 2012; Shu et al., 2016; Huang et al., 2011)]. Our goal is way different from co-segmentation, where geometrically similar parts are detected from a group of object instances within the same category. Their resulting segments are not necessarily coincident with human-interpretable semantics, and these methods need to work on a group of objects, limiting their applicability (see our comparison). Unlike co-segmentation methods that are typically unsupervised, 3D semantic segmentation methods, like [(Yu et al., 2019)], train deep neural networks with labelled 3D datasets for shape segmentation. Pre-trained 2D segmentation models can also be utilized for 3D segmentation, as demonstrated by PartSLIP [(Liu et al., 2023b)], PartSLIP++ [(Zhou et al., 2023)], SAMPart3D [(Yang et al., 2024)] and SAMesh [(Tang et al., 2024)]. Additionally, PartField [(Liu et al., 2025)] learns a continuous feature field, where the similarity between features governs the partition of parts.

    3. Overview

    Problem definition.

    We introduce the task of semantic-aware shape abstraction, formally defined as follows: Given an input watertight 3D shape S, a semantic guidance signal g, and a set of geometric primitives {p_box,pₑₗₗᵢₚₛ,pₛₚₕₑᵣₑ,…}, the objective is to generate an abstracted shape Sₐ composed of N primitives that faithfully reconstruct the structure of S while respecting semantic constraints, defined as:

    (1)

    Sₐ=ψ(S,g,{p_box,pₑₗₗᵢₚₛ,pₛₚₕₑᵣₑ,…}).

    Specifically, each primitive in Sₐ must be assigned to a single, unique semantic region indicated by g, with no primitive spanning across different semantic labels (i.e., no cross-semantic placement). See Fig. 2(c) for an illustrative example. The abstraction may consist of primitives of a single type or a mixture thereof. The semantic guidance g can be derived from 2D semantic masks, or from 3D per-vertex or per-face semantic annotations, either manually provided or sourced from existing datasets.

    Our setting and solution.

    In this paper, we instantiate this problem with two modifications: i) only the ellipsoid pₑₗₗᵢₚₛ is used as the operational primitive, due to its flexible analytical expression for differentiability along with adequate representational ability; ii) the semantic guidance signal g is a set of multi-view 2D semantic masks. We assume that all views have the same level of granularity in their segmentation with a known semantic label set of Lₐ labels (e.g., leg, back, armrest, seat for a chair).

    Our setting can be further defined as:

    (2)

    Sₐ=ψ(S,{Iᵢ}^Mᵢ₌₁,{pⁱₑₗₗᵢₚₛ}^Nᵢ₌₁).

    For notation simplicity and without causing confusion, we use pᵢ to denote our primitive. In our setting, each ellipsoid pᵢ is parameterized by θᵢ, consisting of the center position cᵢ and the covariance matrix Mᵢ, and a desired semantic label l_i,j (i.e., the i-th primitive with the j-th label in the semantic set). We aim to find an optimal solution to spatially distribute the ellipsoids while maintaining the label consistency with the input 2D semantic masks. We formulate it as an optimization problem:

    (3)

    θ^⋆,Π^⋆=\arg\minL_g(θ,S)+λLₛ(θ,Π,S)+μL_c(θ),

    where θ={θᵢ} and Π={l_i,j}, and θ^⋆ and Π^⋆ are the resulting optimal ellipsoid parameters and ellipsoid semantic labels. L_g emphasizes the geometric approximation, Lₛ focuses on the semantic consistency, while L_c quantifies the compactness of the abstraction. λ is a balancing weight to trade off between the geometric accuracy and semantic consistency, and μ is a regularization factor to avoid overcomplicated abstractions. Optimizing over both the continuous variables θ and the integer variables Π yields a mixed-integer problem, which is typically non-convex and challenging to solve. We resort to an alternating optimization scheme to tackle this problem iteratively. Briefly, in each iteration, we first solve the optimal semantic label depending on the current abstraction, and then optimize the abstraction based on the obtained semantic label in this round (see Fig. 3). We elaborate on technical details in the following section.

    4. Proposed Method

    Figure 3 displays an overview of our approach. In what follows, we first introduce the pre-processing, the two optimization terms in Eq. 3, followed by the optimization and post-processing.

    Pre-processing.

    Given the input shape S, we begin by evenly sampling 100k 3D points within its volume. We then apply Gaussian Mixture Model (GMM) clustering with cluster number K to group these points into coarse ellipsoidal clusters that respect the underlying geometry. To better handle thin structures (e.g., thin table legs), we additionally evaluate each cluster by computing the ratio between its maximum and minimum axis lengths. If the ratio exceeds a threshold, indicating a highly elongated shape, we recursively apply GMM with cluster number 2 to subdivide the cluster until the ratio criterion is satisfied. We finally estimate a single ellipsoid for each cluster. This process is efficient (∼10s) and yields the initial set of N ellipsoids for the subsequent optimization.

    4.1. Geometric Approximation Term

    Although shape abstraction inevitably sacrifices geometric precision, the abstracted shape should still maintain a reasonable fidelity to the input geometry. To this end, we introduce a geometric approximation term L_g that quantifies the discrepancy between the input shape and its abstraction.

    Specifically, we measure the difference in the occupancy field with a set Ωₛ of sampled points x from the bounding box of the input shape. Following [(Ren et al., 2021)], we exploit SDF-based occupancy approximation for each ellipsoid to ensure differentiability. Concretely, we use approximated analytical SDF expression dⁱ(x)[(Quilez, 2008)] for each pᵢ, its occupancy is then defined as:

    (4)

    Oⁱ(x)=wᵢ·Sigmoid(-ηdⁱ(x)),

    where η controls the sharpness of the approximation, and wᵢ is a weight enabling or disabling pᵢ, optimized together with pᵢ. Thus, for a shape abstraction with N primitives, its occupancy function O_abs is given by:

    (5)

    O_abs(x)=∑ᵢ₌₁^NOⁱ(x)·(e^Oⁱ(x)/ψ)/(∑ⱼ₌₁^Ne^Oʲ(x)/ψ),

    where ψ is the temperature of the softmax function. We define the geometric approximation loss term as:

    (6)

    L_g=(1)/(|Ωₛ|)∑_x∈Ωₛ||Oₛ(x)-O_abs(x)||²₂,

    where Oₛ(x) is the reference occupancy function value of the input shape.

    4.2. Semantic Consistency Term

    The goal of the semantic consistency term is to inject the semantic constraints into the primitive optimization process, measuring the consistency between the multi-view 2D semantic masks {Iᵢ}^Mᵢ₌₁ and the primitive semantic labels. We design a novel differentiable projection-blending-evaluation scheme for this term.

    Differentiable projection.

    The purpose of this projection is to differentiably project each ellipsoid onto each semantic mask image and associate primitives with pixel-wise semantic labels. For differentiable simplicity, we choose the orthographic projection.

    The differentiable perspective projection can be derived analogously, but requires careful implementation to avoid numerical instabilities [(Eberly, 1999)]. Note that we take one primitive pᵢ and one mask image Iᵢ as an example, and omit the subscript for notational simplicity in the following. The projection process applies to all primitives and views. See the inset for an illustration.

    Projecting an ellipsoid, defined as f(x)=(x-c)ᵀM(x-c)-1, onto an image plane will form an ellipse. We aim to find the ellipse equation with ellipsoid parameters, enabling differentiable optimization. Specifically, given a semantic mask I, its plane/view direction is v⃗. We can define a pair of orthogonal local plane axes e₁⊥e₂∈ℝ³. Any 3D point x on the image plane lies on the projected boundary of the ellipse if and only if the viewing ray passing through x is tangent to the ellipsoid:

    (7)(x-c)ᵀM(x-c)-1=0,
    (8)∇f(x)·v⃗=0.

    Substituting Eq. 7 into Eq. 8 results in an intersection image plane passing through the ellipsoid center c:

    (9)

    v⃗ᵀM(x-c)=0.

    This plane intersects with the ellipsoid, forming an oriented spatial ellipse, whose projection is the desired projected ellipse. Then, given any 2D point x_2d on the mask image plane, it can be easily expressed as the corresponding 3D point x as: x=[e₁,e₂]·x_2d+c. A ray going through the 2d point x_2d along the viewing direction: r=x+t·v⃗, intersects with the plane (Eq. 9) at point p*:

    (10)

    p*=(x-c)-(v⃗v⃗ᵀM)/(v⃗ᵀMv⃗)(x-c)+c.

    Finally, if p* lies at the intersected ellipse, we substitute p* into the ellipsoid equation (Eq. 7) to obtain the equation of the projected ellipse:

    (11)

    g(x_2d)=x_2dᵀ·[e₁,e₂]ᵀ(I-(v⃗v⃗ᵀM)/(v⃗ᵀMv⃗))ᵀM(I-(v⃗v⃗ᵀM)/(v⃗ᵀMv⃗))[e₁,e₂]·x_2d-1.

    Similarly, we exploit the SDF-based occupancy approximation for the 2d ellipse. The SDF function of the ellipse can be estimated using the first-order approximation d_2d=g/∥∇g∥, which is further converted into 2D occupancy (O_2d) using the same scheme as Eq. 4.

    Alpha blending.

    Having the 2D occupancy of each ellipsoid, the next step before rendering them into the mask image is the visibility check. A common choice is the z-less checking, where the closest primitive surface will be rendered. However, simply taking the object surface with the smallest z-depth is erroneous in our task, as the primitives are distributed throughout the shape’s volume and often occlude or overlap with one another. Unseen primitives get little chance to be optimized.

    To tackle this occluding issue, instead of simply ignoring fully occluded primitives, which does not utilize depth information and lead to non-smooth optimization, we propose a novel alpha blending scheme. Taking one view for example, given an arbitrary 2d point x_2d on the mask image plane, a ray shooting through it intersects with many primitives. Let the depth at each primitive’s front surface regarding the viewing direction be z=(z₁,z₂,…,z_N), and the corresponding 2D occupancies of all primitives at that point be:

    (12)

    O_2d(x_2d)=(O¹_2d(x_2d),O²_2d(x_2d),…,O^N_2d(x_2d)),

    then the alpha-blended 2D occupancy of primitive i at point x_2d is computed as:

    (13)

    Õ_2dⁱ=Oⁱ_2d(x_2d)×Softmax(z/β)(i).

    The coefficient β is the temperature of the softmax function. Intuitively, high temperature results in a ‘softer’ probability distribution, encouraging all primitives to be visible in the projection, while low temperature leads to a ‘sharper’ probability distribution, concentrating on the primitives with the smallest depth and degenerating to the z-less strategy.

    Semantic penalty evaluation.

    Ideally, each primitive should be assigned with only one label. We record the label assignment with a matrix A, where A[i,j]=1 if primitive i has label j, and 0 otherwise. The penalty of multi-label assignment of a primitive is defined by the overlap between its projected ellipse and all image pixels that belong to other labels:

    (14)

    Lₛₑₘ[i,j]=∑ₘ₌₁^M𝔼_x_2d∼U([-1,1]²)[∑_k≠jI_m,k(x_2d)·Õ_2d^i,m(x_2d)],

    where m is the view/mask image index, I_m,k is the semantic mask of label k at the m-th image/view, U([-1,1]²) defines the image plane, and x_2d is a sampled pixel point, and finally, Õ_2d^i,m(x_2d) is Eq. 13 at view m. The overall penalty for all primitives across all views is defined as:

    (15)

    Lₛ=(1)/(N×Lₐ)∑_i,j^N,LₐLₛₑₘ[i,j]×A[i,j].

    4.3. Compactness Term

    Compactness, i.e., approximating the shape using as few primitives as possible, is also a desirable property. We introduce another compactness loss to prune redundant primitives by pushing their wᵢ to zero:

    (16)

    L_c=1/N∑ᵢ₌₁^Nwᵢ.

    After the optimization ends, we discard all primitives with wᵢ<0.5.

    4.4. Iterative optimization

    As shown in Eq. 15, the label assignment matrix A contributes to evaluating the semantic penalty. However, solving the integer variables in A and the continuous variables for the primitive parameters is impractical and not stable. We thus solve our optimization, defined in Eq. 3, with two alternating steps.

    Step I - Label assignment.

    A valid label assignment must satisfy the following three conditions: i) each primitive is assigned exactly one label, ii) each label is assigned to at least one primitive, and iii) the overall semantic penalty is minimized. Thus, starting from the initialized primitives and the multi-view mask images, we solve the following constrained integer linear programming:

    Π^*=argmin∑ᵢⱼA[i,j]×Lₛₑₘ[i,j]

    (17)

    s.t. ∀j∑ᵢA[i,j]>0∧∀i∑ⱼA[i,j]=1.

    The optimization only contains N×Lₐ variables, and can be solved with little overhead in practice.

    Step II - Primitive optimization.

    After the label assignment optimization, we obtain optimal labels A for all primitives, and then optimize our objective:

    (18)\beginsplitL&=(1)/(|Ωₛ|)∑_x∈Ωₛ||Oₛ(x)-O_abs(x)||²₂ &+λ/LₐN∑_i,j^N,LₐLₛₑₘ[i,j]×A[i,j] &+μ/N∑ᵢ₌₁^Nwᵢ,\endsplit

    with gradient-based optimization only on continuous parameters.

    In the next round, the previous primitive configuration serves as the input to optimize the labels, while the new label assignment supports the computation of the semantic penalty term. We alternately optimize the two in an iterative manner until it reaches a maximum iteration number.

    Post-merging

    Similar to existing shape abstraction methods such as Marching-Primitives, the primitive numbers in our method is controlled implicitly through the number of initial clusters and the compactness loss weight μ, rather than constrained to a budget. To recover the shape without much geometry sacrifice, we use N around 40∼120. In the post-processing step, we provide a stable way to further reduce the primitive numbers while strictly conforming to the semantic labels obtained from the optimization. Briefly, it contains three steps. Given the N primitives with their unique labels, at step one, we detect connected components within each semantic label. For example, four connected components can be found for the four legs of a chair. At step two, within each connected component, we recursively merge primitives into a bigger cluster if the volume of the oriented bounding box (OBB) of their merged shape is below a threshold ratio (i.e., 2.0) compared against the sum of their volumes. At step three, we collect all the merged clusters, initialize an ellipsoid for each of them, and run a few (∼500) primitive parameter optimization steps (i.e., Step II) adhering to their unique labels. Note that the default ratio threshold can lead to around 3x primitive reduction (Fig. 4), and by tuning the threshold, we can achieve multi-level abstractions.

SemEllipsoid: Semantic-aware Shape Abstraction with Ellipsoid

Abstract.

Representing 3D shapes using a set of primitives–known as shape abstraction–is an actively studied problem in computer graphics. with wide applications in shape understanding, analysis, and simulation due to the compactness and computational efficiency of the primitive-based representation. Prior work has primarily focused on geometry-aware shape abstraction, where the objective is to approximate the input shape with a minimal set of primitives while preserving geometric fidelity. However, these methods often overlook semantic consistency, inevitably leading to primitives that span across multiple semantic parts. Such inconsistency can cause undesirable artifacts in downstream tasks such as part-level shape editing or manipulation. In this paper, we introduce a new task - semantic-aware shape abstraction, where the goal is to produce abstractions that are both geometrically faithful and semantically consistent, ensuring that each primitive adheres strictly to a single semantic part without crossing semantic boundaries. We propose SemEllipsoid, a novel method to address this problem using ellipsoidal primitives. The core idea is to inject semantic constraints into the primitive optimization process leveraging the availability of semantic cues from large-scale foundation models. We design a fully differentiable projection–blending–evaluation scheme to measure semantic divergence against input semantic masks, and formulate an alternating optimization strategy to iteratively solve for optimal semantic assignment and primitive configurations. Our method is non-learning-based, requiring no data collection or network training, and generalizes well to shapes from arbitrary categories. It also supports different levels of abstraction according to user demand. Extensive experiments and evaluations validate the effectiveness of our approach across several 3D shape collections.

Keywords:

Shape Abstraction, Semantic Injection, Primitives, Ellipsoid, Differentiable Projection-Blending-Evaluation

1. Introduction

Humans perceive real-world objects by effortlessly recognizing their structure by parts and part semantics, serving as important cues for many purposes, like human-object interaction and object functionality analysis. The structure can be represented as a composition of simple primitives (e.g., spheres, ellipsoids, boxes) with clear semantics. The decomposition and abstraction process, also known as Shape Abstraction, has been an active research field for decades in computer graphics. The abstract shape, its structures, and part semantics play an essential role in downstream tasks, such as shape geometry, structure and functionality analysis [(Mitra et al., 2014; Hu et al., 2018)], shape editing [(Yumer et al., 2015)], shape retrieval and manipulation [(Sun et al., 2019)], object grasping [(Vezzani et al., 2017; Vezzani et al., 2018)], and motion planning [(Ruan et al., 2022)].

Existing research solves this problem from different aspects - computational optimization [(Chevalier et al., 2003; Vaskevicius and Birk, 2017)], deep learning [(Tulsiani et al., 2017; Sun et al., 2019; Zhao et al., 2024)], to name a few. More recent work (e.g., PrimitiveAnything [(Ye et al., 2025)], PartGen [(Chen et al., 2025a)]) reformulates this task as shape-conditioned primitive generation. Their training is performed on a human-annotated large-scale dataset, improving the generalization ability greatly. The primary focus of prior work is geometry-aware shape abstraction, where the objective is to approximate the input shape with a minimal set of primitives while preserving geometric fidelity. However, these methods often overlook semantic consistency, inevitably leading to primitives that span across multiple semantic parts. Such inconsistency can cause undesirable artifacts in downstream tasks such as part-level shape editing or manipulation. Figure 2 presents such an example, where Marching-Primitives [(Liu et al., 2023a)] outputs a superquadrics abstraction of the back leg, spanning from the leg to the back (Fig. 2(a)). A follow-up part-based shape editing produces undesired artifacts (Fig. 2(b)).

In this paper, we propose a new task–semantic-aware shape abstraction, where the goal is to produce abstractions that are both geometrically faithful and semantically consistent, ensuring that each primitive adheres strictly to a single semantic part without crossing semantic boundaries (see Fig. 2(c)). Two core challenges exist to achieve this goal: i) where to obtain the semantic information, and ii) how to inject the semantic cues during shape abstraction. We draw inspiration from the rapid advancement of large foundation models. For example, Segment Anything Model (SAM) [(Kirillov et al., 2023)] and DINO [(Zhang et al., 2022)] can produce part semantics robustly and accurately, making semantic information readily accessible in a category-agnostic and open-vocabulary manner.

Based on this insight, we present a novel approach, dubbed SemEllipsoid, for semantic-aware shape abstraction with ellipsoids. Our approach falls into the category of geometrical optimization-based shape abstraction, and we achieve semantic injection by formulating it as a semantic penalty loss term in the optimization. Specifically, given an input 3D shape together with multi-view semantic masks, we first initialize a set of ellipsoid primitives to approximate the input. In the following optimization, we aim to simultaneously find the optimal primitive parameters and semantic labels, such that the primitives resemble the shape with high geometric fidelity while strictly adhering to semantic constraints.

To measure the semantic discrepancy, we choose to project the ellipsoid to the semantic masks. However, primitives inside the shape volume occlude and overlap with each other. Naive projection will simply disable the optimization for inside primitives. Given the non-linear and non-convex nature of the optimization due to the integer variables of labels and continuous variables of primitives, we solve it iteratively in an alternating way, i.e., label assignment and primitive optimization.   • •

    We propose semantic-aware shape abstraction, a new task for both geometrically faithful and semantically consistent shape abstraction.

  • •

    We propose the first approach-SemEllipsoid, which is simple, neat, and effective for solving this new problem. Our approach can handle various shape categories without any label-intensive data processing and network training, and it can produce multi-level shape abstractions, facilitating various downstream tasks.

    Our projection-blending-evaluation technical design effectively injects semantic cues in a differentiable way, and might inspire future research.

In contrast, we explicitly enforce semantic awareness in our optimization, which can be applied to any input shape without any training process.     Sₐ=ψ(S,g,{p_box,pₑₗₗᵢₚₛ,pₛₚₕₑᵣₑ,…}).
