The semantic guidance g can be derived from 2D semantic masks, or from 3D per-vertex or per-face semantic annotations, either manually provided or sourced from existing datasets.

    Our setting and solution.

    In this paper, we instantiate this problem with two modifications: i) only the ellipsoid pₑₗₗᵢₚₛ is used as the operational primitive, due to its flexible analytical expression for differentiability along with adequate representational ability; ii) the semantic guidance signal g is a set of multi-view 2D semantic masks. We assume that all views have the same level of granularity in their segmentation with a known semantic label set of Lₐ labels (e.g., leg, back, armrest, seat for a chair).

    Our setting can be further defined as:

    (2)

    Sₐ=ψ(S,{Iᵢ}^Mᵢ₌₁,{pⁱₑₗₗᵢₚₛ}^Nᵢ₌₁).

    For notation simplicity and without causing confusion, we use pᵢ to denote our primitive. In our setting, each ellipsoid pᵢ is parameterized by θᵢ, consisting of the center position cᵢ and the covariance matrix Mᵢ, and a desired semantic label l_i,j (i.e., the i-th primitive with the j-th label in the semantic set). We aim to find an optimal solution to spatially distribute the ellipsoids while maintaining the label consistency with the input 2D semantic masks. We formulate it as an optimization problem:

    (3)

    θ^⋆,Π^⋆=\arg\minL_g(θ,S)+λLₛ(θ,Π,S)+μL_c(θ),

    where θ={θᵢ} and Π={l_i,j}, and θ^⋆ and Π^⋆ are the resulting optimal ellipsoid parameters and ellipsoid semantic labels. L_g emphasizes the geometric approximation, Lₛ focuses on the semantic consistency, while L_c quantifies the compactness of the abstraction. λ is a balancing weight to trade off between the geometric accuracy and semantic consistency, and μ is a regularization factor to avoid overcomplicated abstractions. Optimizing over both the continuous variables θ and the integer variables Π yields a mixed-integer problem, which is typically non-convex and challenging to solve. We resort to an alternating optimization scheme to tackle this problem iteratively. Briefly, in each iteration, we first solve the optimal semantic label depending on the current abstraction, and then optimize the abstraction based on the obtained semantic label in this round (see Fig. 3). We elaborate on technical details in the following section.

    4. Proposed Method

    Figure 3 displays an overview of our approach. In what follows, we first introduce the pre-processing, the two optimization terms in Eq. 3, followed by the optimization and post-processing.

    Pre-processing.

    Given the input shape S, we begin by evenly sampling 100k 3D points within its volume. We then apply Gaussian Mixture Model (GMM) clustering with cluster number K to group these points into coarse ellipsoidal clusters that respect the underlying geometry. To better handle thin structures (e.g., thin table legs), we additionally evaluate each cluster by computing the ratio between its maximum and minimum axis lengths. If the ratio exceeds a threshold, indicating a highly elongated shape, we recursively apply GMM with cluster number 2 to subdivide the cluster until the ratio criterion is satisfied. We finally estimate a single ellipsoid for each cluster. This process is efficient (∼10s) and yields the initial set of N ellipsoids for the subsequent optimization.

    4.1. Geometric Approximation Term

    Although shape abstraction inevitably sacrifices geometric precision, the abstracted shape should still maintain a reasonable fidelity to the input geometry. To this end, we introduce a geometric approximation term L_g that quantifies the discrepancy between the input shape and its abstraction.

    Specifically, we measure the difference in the occupancy field with a set Ωₛ of sampled points x from the bounding box of the input shape. Following [(Ren et al., 2021)], we exploit SDF-based occupancy approximation for each ellipsoid to ensure differentiability. Concretely, we use approximated analytical SDF expression dⁱ(x)[(Quilez, 2008)] for each pᵢ, its occupancy is then defined as:

    (4)

    Oⁱ(x)=wᵢ·Sigmoid(-ηdⁱ(x)),

    where η controls the sharpness of the approximation, and wᵢ is a weight enabling or disabling pᵢ, optimized together with pᵢ. Thus, for a shape abstraction with N primitives, its occupancy function O_abs is given by:

    (5)

    O_abs(x)=∑ᵢ₌₁^NOⁱ(x)·(e^Oⁱ(x)/ψ)/(∑ⱼ₌₁^Ne^Oʲ(x)/ψ),

    where ψ is the temperature of the softmax function. We define the geometric approximation loss term as:

    (6)

    L_g=(1)/(|Ωₛ|)∑_x∈Ωₛ||Oₛ(x)-O_abs(x)||²₂,

    where Oₛ(x) is the reference occupancy function value of the input shape.

    4.2. Semantic Consistency Term

    The goal of the semantic consistency term is to inject the semantic constraints into the primitive optimization process, measuring the consistency between the multi-view 2D semantic masks {Iᵢ}^Mᵢ₌₁ and the primitive semantic labels. We design a novel differentiable projection-blending-evaluation scheme for this term.

    Differentiable projection.

    The purpose of this projection is to differentiably project each ellipsoid onto each semantic mask image and associate primitives with pixel-wise semantic labels. For differentiable simplicity, we choose the orthographic projection.

    The differentiable perspective projection can be derived analogously, but requires careful implementation to avoid numerical instabilities [(Eberly, 1999)]. Note that we take one primitive pᵢ and one mask image Iᵢ as an example, and omit the subscript for notational simplicity in the following. The projection process applies to all primitives and views. See the inset for an illustration.

    Projecting an ellipsoid, defined as f(x)=(x-c)ᵀM(x-c)-1, onto an image plane will form an ellipse. We aim to find the ellipse equation with ellipsoid parameters, enabling differentiable optimization. Specifically, given a semantic mask I, its plane/view direction is v⃗. We can define a pair of orthogonal local plane axes e₁⊥e₂∈ℝ³. Any 3D point x on the image plane lies on the projected boundary of the ellipse if and only if the viewing ray passing through x is tangent to the ellipsoid:

    (7)(x-c)ᵀM(x-c)-1=0,
    (8)∇f(x)·v⃗=0.

    Substituting Eq. 7 into Eq. 8 results in an intersection image plane passing through the ellipsoid center c:

    (9)

    v⃗ᵀM(x-c)=0.

    This plane intersects with the ellipsoid, forming an oriented spatial ellipse, whose projection is the desired projected ellipse. Then, given any 2D point x_2d on the mask image plane, it can be easily expressed as the corresponding 3D point x as: x=[e₁,e₂]·x_2d+c. A ray going through the 2d point x_2d along the viewing direction: r=x+t·v⃗, intersects with the plane (Eq. 9) at point p*:

    (10)

    p*=(x-c)-(v⃗v⃗ᵀM)/(v⃗ᵀMv⃗)(x-c)+c.

    Finally, if p* lies at the intersected ellipse, we substitute p* into the ellipsoid equation (Eq. 7) to obtain the equation of the projected ellipse:

    (11)

    g(x_2d)=x_2dᵀ·[e₁,e₂]ᵀ(I-(v⃗v⃗ᵀM)/(v⃗ᵀMv⃗))ᵀM(I-(v⃗v⃗ᵀM)/(v⃗ᵀMv⃗))[e₁,e₂]·x_2d-1.

    Similarly, we exploit the SDF-based occupancy approximation for the 2d ellipse. The SDF function of the ellipse can be estimated using the first-order approximation d_2d=g/∥∇g∥, which is further converted into 2D occupancy (O_2d) using the same scheme as Eq. 4.

    Alpha blending.

    Having the 2D occupancy of each ellipsoid, the next step before rendering them into the mask image is the visibility check. A common choice is the z-less checking, where the closest primitive surface will be rendered. However, simply taking the object surface with the smallest z-depth is erroneous in our task, as the primitives are distributed throughout the shape’s volume and often occlude or overlap with one another. Unseen primitives get little chance to be optimized.

    To tackle this occluding issue, instead of simply ignoring fully occluded primitives, which does not utilize depth information and lead to non-smooth optimization, we propose a novel alpha blending scheme. Taking one view for example, given an arbitrary 2d point x_2d on the mask image plane, a ray shooting through it intersects with many primitives. Let the depth at each primitive’s front surface regarding the viewing direction be z=(z₁,z₂,…,z_N), and the corresponding 2D occupancies of all primitives at that point be:

    (12)

    O_2d(x_2d)=(O¹_2d(x_2d),O²_2d(x_2d),…,O^N_2d(x_2d)),

    then the alpha-blended 2D occupancy of primitive i at point x_2d is computed as:

    (13)

    Õ_2dⁱ=Oⁱ_2d(x_2d)×Softmax(z/β)(i).

    The coefficient β is the temperature of the softmax function. Intuitively, high temperature results in a ‘softer’ probability distribution, encouraging all primitives to be visible in the projection, while low temperature leads to a ‘sharper’ probability distribution, concentrating on the primitives with the smallest depth and degenerating to the z-less strategy.

    Semantic penalty evaluation.

    Ideally, each primitive should be assigned with only one label. We record the label assignment with a matrix A, where A[i,j]=1 if primitive i has label j, and 0 otherwise. The penalty of multi-label assignment of a primitive is defined by the overlap between its projected ellipse and all image pixels that belong to other labels:

    (14)

    Lₛₑₘ[i,j]=∑ₘ₌₁^M𝔼_x_2d∼U([-1,1]²)[∑_k≠jI_m,k(x_2d)·Õ_2d^i,m(x_2d)],

    where m is the view/mask image index, I_m,k is the semantic mask of label k at the m-th image/view, U([-1,1]²) defines the image plane, and x_2d is a sampled pixel point, and finally, Õ_2d^i,m(x_2d) is Eq. 13 at view m. The overall penalty for all primitives across all views is defined as:

    (15)

    Lₛ=(1)/(N×Lₐ)∑_i,j^N,LₐLₛₑₘ[i,j]×A[i,j].

    4.3. Compactness Term

    Compactness, i.e., approximating the shape using as few primitives as possible, is also a desirable property. We introduce another compactness loss to prune redundant primitives by pushing their wᵢ to zero:

    (16)

    L_c=1/N∑ᵢ₌₁^Nwᵢ.

    After the optimization ends, we discard all primitives with wᵢ<0.5.

    4.4. Iterative optimization

    As shown in Eq. 15, the label assignment matrix A contributes to evaluating the semantic penalty. However, solving the integer variables in A and the continuous variables for the primitive parameters is impractical and not stable. We thus solve our optimization, defined in Eq. 3, with two alternating steps.

    Step I - Label assignment.

    A valid label assignment must satisfy the following three conditions: i) each primitive is assigned exactly one label, ii) each label is assigned to at least one primitive, and iii) the overall semantic penalty is minimized. Thus, starting from the initialized primitives and the multi-view mask images, we solve the following constrained integer linear programming:

    Π^*=argmin∑ᵢⱼA[i,j]×Lₛₑₘ[i,j]

    (17)

    s.t. ∀j∑ᵢA[i,j]>0∧∀i∑ⱼA[i,j]=1.

    The optimization only contains N×Lₐ variables, and can be solved with little overhead in practice.

    Step II - Primitive optimization.

    After the label assignment optimization, we obtain optimal labels A for all primitives, and then optimize our objective:

    (18)\beginsplitL&=(1)/(|Ωₛ|)∑_x∈Ωₛ||Oₛ(x)-O_abs(x)||²₂ &+λ/LₐN∑_i,j^N,LₐLₛₑₘ[i,j]×A[i,j] &+μ/N∑ᵢ₌₁^Nwᵢ,\endsplit

    with gradient-based optimization only on continuous parameters.

    In the next round, the previous primitive configuration serves as the input to optimize the labels, while the new label assignment supports the computation of the semantic penalty term. We alternately optimize the two in an iterative manner until it reaches a maximum iteration number.

    Post-merging

    Similar to existing shape abstraction methods such as Marching-Primitives, the primitive numbers in our method is controlled implicitly through the number of initial clusters and the compactness loss weight μ, rather than constrained to a budget. To recover the shape without much geometry sacrifice, we use N around 40∼120. In the post-processing step, we provide a stable way to further reduce the primitive numbers while strictly conforming to the semantic labels obtained from the optimization. Briefly, it contains three steps. Given the N primitives with their unique labels, at step one, we detect connected components within each semantic label. For example, four connected components can be found for the four legs of a chair. At step two, within each connected component, we recursively merge primitives into a bigger cluster if the volume of the oriented bounding box (OBB) of their merged shape is below a threshold ratio (i.e., 2.0) compared against the sum of their volumes. At step three, we collect all the merged clusters, initialize an ellipsoid for each of them, and run a few (∼500) primitive parameter optimization steps (i.e., Step II) adhering to their unique labels. Note that the default ratio threshold can lead to around 3x primitive reduction (Fig. 4), and by tuning the threshold, we can achieve multi-level abstractions.
